title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
prompt: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeating characters. A substring is a contiguous run of characters (not a subsequence). Return just the length.
blurb: The canonical variable-size sliding window — grow the right edge, and jump the left edge past the last occurrence of any repeat.

rubric.label: Problem understanding
rubric.description: Distinguishes substring (contiguous) from subsequence, confirms the return is a length not the substring, and asks about the character set (ASCII vs full Unicode).

rubric.label: Approach
rubric.description: Reaches the sliding window with a last-seen-index map; recognizes that on a repeat the left edge can jump directly to last_seen+1 rather than crawling one step at a time.

rubric.label: Correctness
rubric.description: Only advances left forward (never backward) using left = max(left, last_seen[c]+1) — otherwise a stale earlier index can shrink the window incorrectly; updates last_seen[c] every step and tracks the running max.

rubric.label: Complexity analysis
rubric.description: O(n) time — each character enters and leaves the window at most once (amortized, not nested); O(min(n, alphabet)) space for the map.

rubric.label: Code quality
rubric.description: Single loop over the right edge, one map, one max — no inner rescans; clear names for the window bounds.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Empty string (0), single character (1), all identical ('bbbb' -> 1), all distinct (n), repeat that is outside the current window (must not move left back), spaces/symbols.

rubric.label: Testing
rubric.description: Tests the 'repeat outside the window' trap (e.g. 'abba') that breaks the naive left = last_seen+1 without the max, not just 'abcabcbb'.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Names it as a sliding window up front and explains why the amortized cost is O(n) despite two moving pointers.

constraints: s may contain letters, digits, symbols, and spaces
Answer is the LENGTH of the longest repeat-free substring

examples.explanation: The answer is "abc", length 3. When the second 'a' arrives, the window slides forward off the first 'a'.
Every character repeats immediately, so the longest repeat-free substring is any single "b".
"wke" has length 3. Note "pwke" is a subsequence, not a substring, so it does not count.

test_cases.expected: 2 — the trap: when the final 'a' repeats, its last index (0) is behind left; left must NOT jump backward. Correct windows are 'ab' and 'ab' -> 2
3 — 'vdf'; the earlier 'd' is outside the window when the second 'd' is processed
5 — 'mzuxt'; the repeated 't' at the end is far outside the window
1 — a single space is a valid character

reference.optimal_time: O(n) — one pass, each index visited by the right edge once and by the left edge at most once
reference.optimal_space: O(min(n, k)) where k is the alphabet size (at most 128 for ASCII)

approaches.name: brute force (all substrings)
approaches.idea: Enumerate every start i and end j, and for each candidate check with a set whether it has all-unique characters. Cubic overall (O(n^2) substrings times O(n) uniqueness check, or O(n^2) with an incremental set).
approaches.time: O(n^3) naive, O(n^2) with an incremental set

approaches.name: sliding window with a set (crawling left)
approaches.idea: Maintain a window [left, right] and a set of its characters. Extend right; while s[right] is already in the set, remove s[left] and increment left until the duplicate is gone; then add s[right] and update max. Correct and O(n) amortized, but left crawls one step at a time.

approaches.name: optimal: sliding window with last-seen index map
approaches.idea: Store last_seen[c] = most recent index of c. Iterate right from 0..n-1. If s[right] is in the map AND its last index >= left, jump left = last_seen[s[right]] + 1 in one move. Always set last_seen[s[right]] = right and update max = max(max, right - left + 1). The max/guard on left is essential so a repeat that sits BEFORE the current window doesn't drag left backward.

follow_ups: Return the substring itself, not just its length — track the best window's start index alongside the max.
Longest substring with AT MOST k distinct characters — window grows while distinct <= k, shrinks otherwise (count map).
Longest substring with at most TWO distinct characters — the k=2 special case, common as a standalone.
Longest REPEATING character replacement — window valid while (window_len - count_of_most_frequent) <= k allowed replacements.
Minimum window substring — a fixed-target variant that expands to satisfy a requirement then contracts to minimize.
reference.reference_solution: lengthOfLongestSubstring(s): last_seen = {}  // char -> most recent index. left = 0; best = 0. for right in range(len(s)): c = s[right]; if c in last_seen and last_seen[c] >= left: left = last_seen[c] + 1  // jump past the previous occurrence, but only if it's inside the window. last_seen[c] = right; best = max(best, right - left + 1). return best. The guard last_seen[c] >= left (equivalently left = max(left, last_seen[c]+1)) is the subtle correctness point: without it, 'abba' would set left back to 1 when the final 'a' is seen, producing a wrong answer. Each right advances once and left only ever moves forward, so the total work is O(n).
pitfalls: Setting left = last_seen[c] + 1 unconditionally, allowing left to move backward when the repeat is outside the window ('abba', 'tmmzuxt').
Forgetting to update last_seen[c] on every character, not just on repeats.
Computing window length as right - left instead of right - left + 1 (off by one).
Confusing substring with subsequence and trying to keep non-contiguous characters.
Using a set with crawling left and then claiming O(n) while actually rescanning — it is O(n) amortized, but the index-map version avoids the crawl entirely.

interviewer_notes: Let the candidate name the technique. If they start enumerating all substrings, accept the brute force then ask for better; reaching 'sliding window' is the entry signal, and reaching the last-seen-index jump (vs crawling left) is the mid signal. The single most revealing probe is the string 'abba': many candidates write left = last_seen[c] + 1 without the max guard and get it wrong. Don't volunteer this — wait for testing, and if they don't test it, hand it to them and ask for the trace. Push on the amortized O(n) argument if they claim it's O(n^2) because of the two pointers. Once correct, escalate to 'at most k distinct characters', which reuses the window skeleton but flips to a shrink-when-invalid pattern — that transition separates mid from senior.
